Good morning. Imagine you are in a museum. You point your phone at a painting, and a guide tells you its style and the story of that movement. Our museum wants exactly this, on visitors' phones and on kiosks in the galleries. We worked on five styles: Baroque, Cubism, Impressionism, Pop Art and Ukiyo-e. The kiosks have small CPUs, the team is small and the budget is limited. So the director asks one question: is a neural network worth it in production, or would a simpler classical model do the job?

To answer, we went step by step, and each step told us what to try next. Step one: the data, and a fair test. Step two: our own network, a multi-layer perceptron built from PyTorch primitives. Step three: we watched its training from the inside and learned to diagnose failures. Step four: a pretrained convolutional network, ResNet18. Step five: a final test of every model, classical models included. Step six: the cost on a kiosk CPU. At the end of these six steps, we will have our answer. Let's start with the data.

Step one: the data. We took 1 500 paintings from WikiArt, 300 per style. We used the course script with a fixed seed, so anyone can download exactly the same images. We cut them into three piles: 1 061 to train, 219 to validate, that is, to choose our settings, and 220 to test, used only once, at the very end. One rule matters a lot: all the paintings of a known painter go to the same pile. With a random split, 23 of our 32 known painters would be in two piles, and a model could learn to recognise Monet instead of Impressionism. With our split: zero. I will come back to this, because we measured its effect.

Step two: our own network. Our first model is the network of the course: a multi-layer perceptron built from nn.Linear layers and ReLU, with our own training loop. It reads the pixels of a 64 by 64 image: 12 288 inputs and 6.4 million parameters. Before trusting it, we ran two checks. First, a model that knows nothing should have a loss of ln 5, about 1.61. Ours started at 1.99, too confident, so we made its last layer smaller and got 1.59. Second, it must be able to learn one small batch by heart: it does, 100 percent. Then the real training. The training accuracy goes to 99.7 percent, but the validation accuracy stays around 40 percent, and the validation loss goes up after epoch 3. This is overfitting: the network learns the paintings by heart.

Step three: monitoring. We looked inside the network during training, not only at the loss. The gradient reaches every layer and only 4 percent of the neurons are dead: the training is healthy, the problem is overfitting. We also tried 8 learning rates and kept 0.0001. Then we tested the tools of session 6, each with 3 seeds, because one run on 219 images is noisy. Alone, each tool helps a little. All together, weight decay, dropout, batch norm, flips, early stopping and a cosine schedule take the MLP from 38.8 to 45.5 percent, and the gap between train and validation from 0.61 to 0.12. But one number shows the real limit: the MLP finds only 7 percent of the Cubist paintings. It sees colours, not shapes.

Still in step three, we wanted to be ready for problems in production, so we broke the training four times on purpose, and diagnosed each run. A learning rate 100 times too big killed 99.6 percent of the neurons of layer 2. A forgotten zero_grad made the gradients pile up: 26 times bigger after two epochs. Raw pixels, without standardisation, gave a first loss of 16 instead of 1.6. And eight sigmoid layers gave a vanishing gradient: the first layer received less than a millionth of the gradient of the last one. The lesson: two of these bugs show the same symptom, a loss stuck at ln 5. Only the monitoring, dead neurons or the gradient per layer, can tell them apart.

Step four. Our MLP sees colours but not shapes, and to see shapes, we need a convolutional network. With only 1 061 images we cannot train one from zero, so we reuse ResNet18, already trained on 1.2 million ImageNet photos. We freeze it: each painting becomes 512 numbers, and we train only one linear layer, 2 565 weights, in less than a second. Result: 88.1 percent on validation, almost twice our best MLP. We also fine-tuned the last block: 8.4 million weights for 1 061 images. It overfits: 85.4 percent. And we measured two silent bugs: forgetting model.eval() drops the score to 12.8 percent, and forgetting the ImageNet normalisation costs 6 points. Nothing crashes: only measuring shows them.

With this stronger model, we could finally test the painter rule of step one. To measure it fairly, we scored the same images twice with cross-validation, and changed only one thing: whether the model had seen other paintings by the same painter. On images by known painters: 83.7 percent when the painter was seen, 72.3 when not. 11 points of flattery. On the control group, the unknown painters, nothing changes. So the model partly recognises painters, and a random split would have given the director a score that is too good. Our split protects the result.

Step five: the final test. We opened the 220 test paintings once, for every model, including classical models with no neural network, such as a random forest on hand-made colour and texture features. The pretrained models are at the top, from 83 to 88 percent. The random forest reaches 67, our MLP 41. Is the gap real? A paired bootstrap, 5 000 redraws of the same test paintings, gives our model a lead of 16.4 points over the random forest, between 9 and 24 points: it is not luck. One honest note: the fine-tuned model is first on the test, but it was second on validation. With about 220 images, a score moves by about 5 points by chance, so we keep the model we chose before the test.

Step six: is it affordable on a kiosk? We timed one photo at a time, from the image to the answer. The ResNet needs 53 milliseconds on one CPU thread, 26 with four threads: faster than a blink. Even on a kiosk four times slower, it answers in a fifth of a second. The model file is 45 megabytes. And when the collection changes, we only recompute the features and retrain one layer, in seconds.

Let's put the six steps together. On the test, our own MLP reached 41 percent, the best classical model 67, and the frozen ResNet18 83, at a cost a kiosk can afford. So, our answer to the director: yes, a neural network is worth it, but a pretrained one that we reuse. We recommend a frozen ResNet18 with a linear head. Why? It is accurate: one visitor in six gets a wrong style, against one in three. It is fast enough for a modest CPU, and cheap for a small team: one small layer, retrained in seconds. We do not recommend our MLP, a classical model alone, or fine-tuning for now. Before the launch, we must test real photos taken at the kiosks, add more styles, and measure the real hardware. Thank you. We are happy to take your questions.
